# Introduction

The field of reproducible science as implemented in [RStudio](https://rstudio.com/) is moving very fast and it is hard to keep up with new R packages and tools. The instructor is attempting at providing students with relevant online resources to complement class materials.   

# How to Cite These Materials {#howtocite}

**If you use this course's chapters, data or example projects in your own work, cite them.** That includes your bioinformatics tutorial: the rubric asks for references, and material you took from here is a reference like any other.

There are **two** things you might be citing, and they are not the same object:

| What you used | Cite | Why |
|---|---|---|
| the chapters, as you read them | the **course website** | it is the published, readable version |
| the source, the data, the example projects | the **GitHub repository** | it is the thing that holds the files you ran |

## Ready to paste

**Use the first one unless you have a reason not to.** The course materials are archived on Zenodo and have a **DOI**, which is the citation that will still work in ten years, whatever happens to the web addresses.

```
@misc{buerki2026materials,
  author = {Buerki, Sven},
  title  = {{EEB 603 Reproducible Science: course materials}},
  year   = {2026},
  doi    = {10.5281/zenodo.24139921},
  url    = {https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24139921}
}

@misc{buerki2026website,
  author  = {Buerki, Sven},
  title   = {{EEB 603 Reproducible Science: course website}},
  year    = {2026},
  url     = {https://svenbuerki.github.io/EEB603_Reproducible_Science/},
  urldate = {2026-11-11}
}
```

Cite them in your text as `[@buerki2026materials]` and `[@buerki2026website]`. **If you use the second one, change `urldate` to the date you actually consulted the site.**

| Use | When |
|---|---|
| **the DOI entry** | you used the chapters, data or example projects. **This is the normal case** |
| the website entry | you are citing the live site specifically, for instance something that is only on the web version |

<div class="info">
  <p><strong>&#128161; There are two DOIs, and the one above is the right one for you</strong></p>
  <p><code>10.5281/zenodo.24139921</code> is the <b>concept DOI</b>: it always resolves to the most recent archived version, so your reference does not go stale when the course is updated. The <b>version DOI</b> <code>10.5281/zenodo.24139922</code> points at release <code>v1.0.1</code> and nothing else. <b>Use the version DOI when exactness matters</b>, which is the same argument this course makes about recording package versions: cite what you actually used.</p>
</div>

**The repository also carries a `CITATION.cff` file**, which is why GitHub shows a **Cite this repository** button on [its page](https://github.com/svenbuerki/EEB603_Reproducible_Science). That button will generate BibTeX and APA for you, and it is the habit to copy: a repository that says how to cite it gets cited correctly.

## What you may reuse {#licence}

**Two licences cover this course, because it holds two kinds of thing.**

| What | Licence | Full terms |
|---|---|---|
| **Prose and teaching material**: chapter text, figures, slides, rubrics, schedule | [**CC BY 4.0**](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/) | [`LICENSE-CC-BY-4.0.md`](https://github.com/svenbuerki/EEB603_Reproducible_Science/blob/master/LICENSE-CC-BY-4.0.md) |
| **Code**: scripts, R chunks, functions, the site build | [**GNU AGPL v3.0**](https://www.gnu.org/licenses/agpl-3.0.en.html) | [`LICENSE.md`](https://github.com/svenbuerki/EEB603_Reproducible_Science/blob/master/LICENSE.md) |

**CC BY 4.0 asks three things of you**: credit the author, link to the licence, and say if you changed anything. You may adapt the material, and you may use it commercially. So you are free to reuse a chapter in your own teaching, provided you say where it came from, and the BibTeX above is how you do that.

**This is the split from [Creative Commons Licenses](Chapters.html#CClicenses) applied to this course itself**: a CC licence for what you read, a software licence for what you run. A single licence covering both would mean using the wrong instrument for half of it.

## Three rules that decide whether your reference is usable

These are not style preferences. Each one was checked by knitting the entry and reading the output:

1. **Use `url = {...}`, never `howpublished = {\url{...}}`.** With `howpublished`, the URL is **silently dropped** from the reference list: the entry still renders, it just no longer says where the thing is. This is the single most common reason a web citation comes out unusable.
2. **Add `urldate = {YYYY-MM-DD}`.** A website is a living document. The access date is what tells a reader which version you saw.
3. **`version` and `note` are ignored** by most styles, so do not put the version there. If you need to name a version, put it in the title.
4. **Protect your capitalisation with double braces.** Most journal styles, including this course's, apply **sentence case** to titles: they lowercase everything they were not told to leave alone. Written as `title = {EEB 603 Reproducible Science}` it comes out as *"EEB 603 reproducible science"*. Wrapping the whole title in a second pair of braces, `title = {{EEB 603 Reproducible Science}}`, renders it exactly as you typed it. **This matters for your own references too**: a species name, a gene symbol or an acronym in a title will be quietly lowercased unless you protect it.

## Use the course CSL {#whichcsl}

**Declare `AmJBot.csl` in your YAML**, the same file every document in this course uses. It is in the [repository root](https://github.com/svenbuerki/EEB603_Reproducible_Science/blob/master/AmJBot.csl):

```
csl: AmJBot.csl
```

**This matters more than it sounds.** Many journal styles print nothing at all to locate a website, so the same `.bib` entry that works here becomes a dead reference in another style. Tested with the entries above:

| Citation style | With the **DOI** entry | With the **website** entry |
|---|---|---|
| **`AmJBot.csl`, the course style** | **yes** | **yes**, with the access date |
| IEEE | yes | yes, with the access date |
| APA, Chicago author-date | yes | yes, no access date |
| Nature, Elsevier-Harvard | **yes** | no |
| Ecology, New Phytologist, the official American Journal of Botany style | **no** | **no** |

**Two things to read off that table.** The DOI entry works in six of the nine styles tested and the website entry in four, which is the practical reason to prefer the DOI. And three styles print **nothing** that locates the work in either case, so if your tutorial uses one of them the citation renders and still leaves your reader stuck. **For course materials, use `AmJBot.csl`.**

<div class="info">
  <p><strong>&#128161; Note that the course <code>AmJBot.csl</code> is not the standard American Journal of Botany style</strong></p>
  <p>The official style from the <a href="https://github.com/citation-style-language/styles" target="_blank" rel="noopener">CSL repository</a> drops URLs for web material; the copy in this course does not. If you download "American Journal of Botany" from Zotero's style repository you will get different output from everybody else in the class. <b>Use the file in the course repository.</b></p>
</div>

**And the course's own recurring lesson applies here too: read the knitted output, not the `.bib`.** A citation problem is invisible in the source and obvious in the reference list.

# Library of open-access books

Please find [here](https://bookdown.org) a suite of open-access books written with the R [*bookdown* package](https://github.com/rstudio/bookdown), which are relevant to the EEB603 - Reproducible Science course.

# R keypoints 

Here are three important points for R coding:

1. R’s basic **data types** are [character]{.underline}, [numeric]{.underline}, [integer]{.underline}, [complex]{.underline}, and [logical]{.underline}. Read more about R data types [here](https://www.w3schools.com/r/r_data_types.asp).
2. R’s basic **data structures** include the [vector]{.underline}, [list]{.underline}, [matrix]{.underline}, [data frame]{.underline}, and [factors]{.underline}. Some of these structures require that all members be of the same data type (e.g. vectors, matrices) while others permit multiple data types (e.g. lists, data frames). Read more about R data structures [here](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/data-structures-in-r-programming/).
3. R **objects** may have attributes, such as name, dimension, and class. Read more about R objects [here](https://rstudio-education.github.io/hopr/r-objects.html).

# R Markdown

Markdown is a simple formatting syntax for authoring HTML, PDF, and MS Word documents. For more details on using R Markdown see <http://rmarkdown.rstudio.com>. Please find below additional key resources on this topic:

- **R Markdown: The Definitive Guide:** https://bookdown.org/yihui/rmarkdown/

# Writing books and complex/large documents

R Markdown can be used to produce basic HTML, PDF, and Word documents; however, more complex and larger projects can become difficult to manage in a single R Markdown file. The *bookdown* package addresses this limitation, and offers several key improvements:

- Books and reports can be built from multiple R Markdown files.
- Additional formatting features are added, such as cross-referencing, and numbering of figures, equations, and tables.
- Documents can easily be exported in a range of formats suitable for publishing, including PDF, e-books and HTML websites.

A book dedicated to this topic can be accessed [here](https://bookdown.org/yihui/bookdown/) and the package can be downloaded [here](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=bookdown).

# Notebook

An R Notebook is an R Markdown document with chunks that can be executed independently and interactively, with output visible immediately beneath the input.

You can create a new notebook in RStudio with the menu command `File -> New File -> R Notebook`, or by using the `html_notebook` output type in your document’s YAML metadata.

# Homework assignments on RPubs

A huge number of homework assignments have been published to the website https://RPubs.com (a free publishing platform provided by RStudio), which shows that R Markdown is easy and convenient enough for students to do their homework assignments. As a TA or GA, you might even consider asking your students to complete their homework using R Markdown and publishing them on RPubs!

# Journals

Submitting scientific manuscripts written in R Markdown is still challenging; however the R [*rticles* package](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rticles/index.html) was designed to simplify the creation of documents that conform to submission standards for academic journals. The package provides a suite of custom R Markdown LaTeX formats and templates for the following journals/publishers that are relevant to the EEB program:

- Biometrics articles
- Elsevier journal submissions
- Frontiers articles
- MDPI journal submissions
- PeerJ articles
- PNAS articles
- Royal Society Open Science journal submissions
- Sage journal submissions
- Springer journal submissions
- The R Journal articles
- Taylor & Francis articles

# Preparing literature

The [doi2bib](https://www.doi2bib.org/) web tool allows you to generate BibTex formatted literature from DOIs.  

# Interactive tutorials

The R [*learnr* package](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/learnr/index.html) allows to turn R Markdown documents into interactive tutorials. Tutorials consist of content along with interactive components for checking and reinforcing understanding. Tutorials can include any or all of the following:

- Narrative, figures, illustrations, and equations.
- Code exercises (R code chunks that users can edit and execute directly).
- Quiz questions.
- Videos (currently supported services include YouTube and Vimeo).
- Interactive Shiny components.

Please see the full documentation (with examples) at this url: https://rstudio.github.io/learnr/
